newsitem.title: NORWAY: Poor data seen threatening marine insurance profit.
newsitem.headline: Poor data seen threatening marine insurance profit.

text.p: The profitability and even the survival of marine insurers are threatened unless they can organise consistent reporting of marine statistics across global markets, a leading U.S. underwriter has warned.

Dennis Koruda, vice president of marine underwriting at St Paul Re, told reporters at the International Union of Marine Insurers (IUMI) in Oslo that marine insurers lag behind non-marine in maintaining accurate data across international markets for the various classes of marine insurance -- hull, cargo, offshore, marine liability and protection and indemnity (P&I).

"Marine insurance and reinsurance is considered a global line of business, yet premium and loss statistics vary widely by class and from one country to the next," Koruda said, adding, "The inconsistency of good data undermines the accuracy of this business."
Koruda said that marine insurance is the most difficult to analyse in the U.S. and London markets, which many would assume to be the most advanced markets for collecting data.

"Many factors contribute to the difficulty in capturing true net statistics. Companies and syndicates that write marine business through line slips, insurance pools and associations, and speciality lines compound the problem of measuring the size and profitability of the marine insurance market.

Estimates of the annual net premiums for marine insurance worldwide range as high as $20 billion including $2 billion in reinsurance premiums. "Some companies have recognised the need for actuarial pricing to ensure the long term profitability of their business," Koruda said.
"Consistent and accurate recording of data, together with sound underwriting discipline, is essential for the long-term survival of the marine insurance industry."
